slides.title: Heap and heapq
slides.main: The heap is the standard priority queue: push and pop the most urgent in O(log n).

captions: We need a structure that adds fast and returns the most urgent fast
Each item has a priority; the smaller the number, the more urgent
The most urgent comes out, not the earliest
The standard answer is a heap: push and pop in O(log n), peek in O(1)

body.text: Fifteen exercises: ten warm-ups, your own heapq and four problems.

slides.title: Heap property
slides.main: The root is always the minimum; siblings need no order.

captions: Every node is at most its children
So the root is always the smallest element
No order between siblings: 7 and 4 sit "out of order", and that is fine
Shape: a complete tree, levels filled left to right with no gaps

frames.text: last level fills left to right

captions: The tree is stored level by level, no links
Parent of node 4 is at (4 − 1) // 2 = 1
Children of node 1 are at 2·1 + 1 = 3 and 2·1 + 2 = 4
Three formulas: parent, left child, right child

slides.title: Sift up
slides.main: Swap with the parent while it is larger: at most log n swaps.

captions: Push 0 into a heap of seven
Append: shape is fine, but 0 < parent 7, so the property breaks
Swap with parent: 0 moved up a level
Smaller than parent 3 again: swap once more
Reached the root: heap restored. At most log n swaps

slides.title: Sift down
slides.sub: Pop: last to root, then lower
slides.main: Swap with the smaller child, or the property breaks.

captions: Pop the minimum 0: a hole at the root breaks the shape
Take the last item (7), put it at the root; heap is one shorter
7 exceeds both children (1, 2): swap with the smaller, 1
Children 3 and 4: swap with the smaller again, 3
7 is a leaf: heap restored, at most log n swaps

slides.title: Operations and heapq
slides.main: Push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1).

captions: Push: append and sift up
Pop min: last to root and sift down
Peek at the min: the list's item 0
Combined operations beat two calls in a row

slides.title: Building in O(n)
slides.main: Node heights sum to O(n): about 2n comparisons, not n log n.

captions: Leaves (index 3 on) are already heaps; go from last parent to root
Node 2 (7): smaller child is 2, swap
Node 1 (4): smaller child is 1, swap
Node 0 (9) sinks to a leaf in two swaps
About 2n comparisons: linear time, not n log n

slides.title: Heapsort
slides.sub: Root to the end, then sift
slides.main: O(n log n) time, O(1) memory, but not stable.

captions: Build a max-heap: the largest is at the root
Swap root with last: 9 is in its place
Sift the new root 6 down in the heap minus the last item
Next maximum 8 goes to its place, and so on
n times log n: O(n log n) time, O(1) memory; not stable

frames.text: heap on the left, sorted tail on the right

slides.title: Python specifics
slides.main: Max via minus sign; objects need a counter for order.

captions: heapq is a min-heap on a plain list; item 0 is the minimum
Maximum: store negated numbers, flip the sign on read
Prioritized objects: (priority, counter, object); the counter avoids incomparable objects and keeps ties in order

slides.title: Top k from a stream
slides.main: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory; the root is the k-th largest.

captions: k = 3: the min-heap holds the best three; the root is the smallest of them
A new item above the root replaces it
The heap is always the k largest seen
Each item costs O(log k): O(n log k) total, O(k) memory
Below the root: rejected, heap unchanged

slides.title: Merging k sequences
slides.main: Heap of at most k items: N log k.

captions: The heap holds one head per list
Popped min 1, pushed the next from that list (4)
Popped 2, took 5
Heap of at most k items: a step is O(log k), N log k in all

slides.title: Stream median
slides.main: Lower half in a max-heap, upper in a min-heap; median from the roots.

captions: Lower half in a max-heap, upper half in a min-heap
Heap sizes differ by at most one
Median: root of the larger heap, or the mean of both roots
Adding is O(log n), median is O(1)
Stream 5, 2, 8, 1, 9: median 5

slides.title: Lazy deletion
slides.sub: A priority queue in graph algorithms
slides.main: No decrease-key: push a new entry, skip stale ones.

captions: The heap holds (distance, vertex) pairs
Shorter path to B found: no decrease-key, so push a new entry (2, B)
The old entry (7, B) stays in the heap
On pop we check: stale entry, skip it. That is lazy deletion

frames.text: (7, B): distance to B is already 2

slides.title: How heapq works
slides.sub: Down to a leaf, then up
slides.main: One comparison per level, not two: same property, less work.

captions: Classic: two comparisons per level (child vs child, child vs item)
CPython: the hole sinks to a leaf, one comparison per level
Then the last item rises from the leaf, usually a couple of steps

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.main: Only item 0 is ordered; in-place edits break the heap.

captions: A heap is not a sorted list; printing it to see the order is pointless
Changed an item inside: property broken, so heapify or rebuild
heapq does min only
Equal priorities: add a counter, or comparison reaches the objects
